Below is a concise, full 12‑week summary you can give your client. It integrates the strength program, press/bank-pattern substitutions (no supine), increased push intensity in Phase B with bench‑pattern work, pregnancy‑safe core programming, cardio, nutrition guidance for lean‑mass maintenance, and a safe peak-week alternative instead of a 1RM. Keep monitoring symptoms, use RPE-based progression, and prioritize pelvic‑floor cues and breathing throughout.

Quick client details / constraints
- 30 y/o, advanced lifter, 20 weeks pregnant (OB cleared for moderate strength).
- Contraindications: no supine after week 16, no max attempts (no true 1RM), no contact sports.
- Goals: maintain/slow strength loss, preserve lean mass, keep pressing (bench-feel) and strong core, maintain conditioning.

Program overview (structure)
- Duration: 12 weeks (Phase A Weeks 1–4; Phase B Weeks 5–8; Phase C Weeks 9–12).
- Frequency: 3 gym strength sessions/week (Mon/Wed/Fri suggested) + 2–3 cardio sessions/week (can be done on non-lift days or after lifting at reduced duration).
- Session length: ~45–60 minutes for strength; cardio 20–40 minutes per session.
- Intensity model: RPE-based. Avoid RPE 9–10 and no true 1RM or maximal singles. Heavy top sets in Phase B allowed up to RPE 7–7.5 (occasionally 8 if all safety checks pass).
- Core: short 8–15 minute core circuit after each strength session (standing/tall‑kneeling/quadruped/side‑lying variations only).
- Nutrition: calorie increase for 2nd trimester (+~200–300 kcal/day baseline, tailor to weight/activity), protein 1.4–1.8 g/kg/day, spread protein across meals, ensure prenatal vitamins, DHA, iron/calcium/Vit D as advised by OB. Hydrate and prioritize recovery.
- Cardio: 2–3 low‑impact sessions/week (treadmill incline walking, recumbent bike, elliptical, pool/aquatics). RPE 5–6 mostly; short intervals (RPE 7–7.5) only in Phase B if tolerated.

Progression rules (general)
- Progress conservatively: increase reps, sets, or load by small increments (2–5%) when current work is RPE ≤ 6 for two sessions.
- Prefer increasing volume before intensity. Keep rest 1.5–3 min for compound lifts; 45–90s for accessories.
- Monitor pelvic pressure, urinary leakage, dizziness, bleeding — stop and consult OB if any adverse sign occurs.

Phase A — Foundation & movement quality (Weeks 1–4) — 20–24 weeks gestation
Goal: retain movement quality, breathing/pelvic‑floor coordination, baseline strength.

Weekly pattern (Mon/Wed/Fri)
- Warm-up: 8–10 min bike/walk + shoulder/thoracic mobility + pelvic‑floor breathing
- Main lifts: 2–3 compound moves per session. RPE target main lifts 6–6.5
  - Examples: Goblet squat 3x8; Bulgarian split squat 3x8; Trap‑bar deadlift 3x6–8
- Upper push/pull: Seated DB press 3x8–10; Seated cable row 3x8–10; Incline chest press seated 3x8–10
- Accessories: banded lateral walks, clams, single‑leg RDL 2–3x8–12
- Core (post‑session): tall‑kneeling Pallof 3x8–10 each side; quadruped bird‑dog 3x8 each; side plank on knees 3x15–20s each
- Cardio: 2 sessions/week 20–30 min moderate walking or pool

Phase B — Strength & push emphasis (Weeks 5–8) — 24–28 weeks gestation
Goal: increase pushing intensity and bench‑pattern work, maintain other strength. Keep top RPE submaximal (7–7.5). Include bench-substitutes (seated/incline/landmine).

Weekly pattern (Mon/Wed/Fri) — heavy push on Mon (Session A)
- Warm-up: 8–10 min + mobility + pelvic‑floor breathing
- Session A — Heavy Push Emphasis (Mon)
  - Seated incline DB/barbell press (back supported) 4–5 × 4–6 @ RPE 7–7.5
  - Single‑arm landmine/cable chest press 3 × 6–8 each side @ RPE 7
  - Seated machine chest press 3 × 6–8 @ RPE 7
  - Antagonist: Seated cable row 3 × 8–10
  - Accessories: triceps ext. 3 × 8–12; lateral raises 2 × 10–12
  - Core: standing/tall‑kneeling Pallof press 3–4 × 8–10 each side; farmer carry 3 × 30–60s
- Session B — Lower/hyp/hinge (Wed)
  - Trap‑bar deadlift 4 × 4–6 @ RPE 6.5
  - Bulgarian split squat 3 × 8–10
  - Lat pulldown 3 × 8–10
  - Light seated chest press 2 × 8
  - Core: standing single‑arm cable anti‑rotation 3 × 8 each; side plank on knees 3 × 20–30s
- Session C — Full body/press maintenance (Fri)
  - Front-loaded goblet or safety‑bar squat 3 × 6–8
  - Chest‑supported single‑arm row 3 × 8 each
  - Standing cable incline press / chest‑supported incline press 3 × 5–6 @ RPE 7
  - Face pulls, farmer carries, posterior chain accessory work
  - Core: banded anti‑extension 3 × 8–10; loaded bird‑dog 3 × 8 each
- Cardio: 2–3 sessions/week (one interval session permitted with short efforts 30–60s at RPE 7) — total moderate work 25–35 min

Phase B progression notes
- Increase load modestly (2–5%) or add a set or 1–2 reps weekly if RPE remains ≤ 6–7.
- Heavy push top sets targeted RPE 7–7.5 (rarely 8). Avoid RPE 9–10 and any heavy single attempts.
- Maintain pelvic‑floor checks, lengthen rest between heavy push sets (2–3 min).

Phase C — Maintenance & preparation for postpartum (Weeks 9–12) — 28–32 weeks gestation
Goal: maintain strength and control; prioritize comfort, mobility, and core endurance. Peak week uses safe submaximal test instead of 1RM.

- Warm-up and breathing as before
- Lifts: keep main lifts at 3 sets × 6–8 @ RPE 6–7; reduce overall volume if fatigue rises
  - Example: Safety‑bar/goblet squat 3 × 6–8; Trap‑bar deadlift 3 × 5–6; Single‑leg RDL 3 × 8; Seated incline press 3 × 6–8
- Press maintenance across sessions with seated/incline presses, landmine presses and cable work
- Accessories: posterior chain, glute medius and shoulder health work; farmer carries for core endurance
- Core: maintain Pallof presses, side planks, bird‑dogs, anti‑extension work (2–3 exercises per session)
- Cardio: prefer pool/aqua (excellent late pregnancy), recumbent bike or walking 20–30 min; reduce intervals — mostly moderate

Week 12 — Peak week (safe protocol; no 1RM)
- Do NOT perform a true 1RM. Use a conservative peak protocol:
  - Warm-up thoroughly.
  - Choose up to 2 primary lifts (e.g., trap‑bar deadlift and seated incline press).
  - Work-up: 6 × 6 @ RPE 6, 4 × 4 @ RPE 6.5, 3 × 3 @ RPE 7, top set 3 reps @ RPE 7.5–8 (stop there). No singles, no maximal attempts.
  - Use top 3‑rep as estimate for progress tracking; estimate 1RM conservatively (e.g., 3RM × 1.06).
  - Keep rest 2.5–3.5 min between heavier sets; monitor symptoms.
- Reduce accessory volume; emphasize recovery, mobility and pelvic‑floor breathing post-session.

Core program (integrated each strength day; 8–15 min)
- Phase A: tall‑kneeling Pallof press, quadruped bird‑dog, side plank on knees (3× per exercise)
- Phase B: heavier Pallof presses (cable), banded anti‑extension rollouts (tall kneel), farmer/suitcase carries, loaded bird‑dog (3–4×)
- Phase C: maintenance core — standing Pallof, side plank variations, bird‑dog, carries (moderate volume)
- Daily pelvic‑floor breathing drills (2–3 min) and small quick gentle pelvic‑floor activations (6–8 quick flicks) — avoid forced max holds.

Cardio plan (2–3 sessions/week)
- Phase A: 2 sessions × 20–30 min moderate (incline treadmill walk, recumbent bike, pool)
- Phase B: 2–3 sessions × 25–35 min with optional short intervals (30–60s at RPE 7) only if tolerated
- Phase C: 2 sessions × 20–30 min prioritizing pool/aqua and walking; reduce intensity if fatigue rises
- Use talk test and RPE (moderate = 5–6/10). Hydrate and avoid overheating.

Nutrition & recovery (summary)
- Calories: increase ~200–300 kcal/day in 2nd trimester as baseline; adjust to weight gain guidance and activity. Monitor weight gain every 1–2 weeks and adjust ±100–300 kcal as needed.
- Protein: 1.4–1.8 g/kg/day (aim for upper end to preserve lean mass). Spread across meals (25–35 g protein/meal).
- Carbs/fats: fuel workouts with 30–60 g carbs around sessions; include healthy fats and DHA (200–300 mg/day from fish/supplement).
- Micronutrients: prenatal vitamin, iron as needed, calcium ~1000 mg/day, vitamin D per OB, iodine as recommended.
- Hydration: ≥2–2.5 L baseline; more with sweat. Avoid overheating, keep cool environment.
- Sleep: 7–9 hours; naps if needed. Recovery between heavy push days: 48–72 hours ideal.
- Refer to pelvic‑floor physio for any incontinence, pelvic pain, diastasis concerns.

Safety & red flags (stop exercise and seek care)
- Vaginal bleeding, regular painful contractions, decreased fetal movement, chest pain, sudden severe shortness of breath, dizziness/fainting, sudden severe swelling, or fluid leakage.
- New or worsening pelvic heaviness, urinary incontinence, or sharp pelvic/abdominal pain — reduce load and consult pelvic health professional.

Coaching cues & practical notes
- Never supine after week 16: use supported incline/seated options for presses and chest work.
- No heavy Valsalva: inhale on eccentric, exhale on concentric while maintaining gentle pelvic‑floor engagement.
- Progress conservatively; small increases in load or reps weekly if RPE allows.
- Document RPE, loads and symptoms each session.
- Use machines and chest‑supported variations for heavier work when balance is a concern.
- Use a spotter for heavier seated/incline barbell work if available and safe.

Testing & postpartum plan
- No true 1RM testing during pregnancy. Use submaximal 3–5 rep top sets to estimate 1RM if desired.
- Plan formal 1RM testing postpartum only after OB clearance and pelvic‑floor rehab as needed (commonly 3–6+ months postpartum depending on recovery).

If you want next steps

- I can create a postpartum testing and return‑to‑max protocol for after delivery.

It respects the stated contraindications (no supine after week 16, no max attempts, no contact sports) and prioritizes safety, joint comfort, pelvic floor integrity, and fatigue management. Individual symptoms and day-to-day variation are expected in pregnancy, so use the RPE guidance and adjustments noted.

Key principles and precautions (read first)
- No supine exercises after 16 weeks: replace with supported upright, seated, or side-lying variations. Avoid Valsalva and breath-holding; cue diaphragmatic breathing and exhale with exertion. Keep loads submaximal (RPE 6–7/10 for main work, avoid true maximal sets).
- Avoid high-impact and contact activities. Monitor balance and center-of-gravity changes; use a spotter or safety rails when needed.
- Emphasize pelvic floor awareness: avoid repeated maximal or forced pelvic floor contractions; instead encourage gentle pre-activation and coordinated breathing. If any urinary leakage, pelvic heaviness, or pain appears, reduce load and consult pelvic health physiotherapist.
- Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE) guidance used below: 6–7/10 = challenging but sustainable; 7–8 occasionally for short sets; never 9–10 maximal.
- Hydration, temperature regulation and frequent rest breaks are important. Stop if dizziness, bleeding, chest pain, regular painful contractions, or reduced fetal movement occur.
- Progress conservatively: increase load when current working sets feel RPE 6/10 for two sessions in a row. Prefer more reps and better control over bigger jumps in weight.
- Warm-up and cool-down are included each session.

Structure overview
- 12 weeks total: Weeks 1–4 (Phase A — Foundation & movement quality), Weeks 5–8 (Phase B — Strength emphasis, conservative load increase), Weeks 9–12 (Phase C — Maintenance and preparation for postpartum transition).
- Frequency: 3 gym sessions/week (full-body focused), plus optional gentle cardio/walking and mobility work on off days. Keep session length ~45–60 minutes.
- Each gym session: warm-up (8–10 min), main lifts (2–3 compound movements), accessory work (2–4 exercises), pelvic floor/core-friendly work, mobility/cool-down. Use supersets where sensible (antagonist pairing or upper/lower) to save time and avoid prolonged fatigue.
- Load prescription expressed as sets x reps @ RPE; replace %1RM guidance with RPE and conservative progressive overload.

Weekly layout (example)
- Monday: Session A — Lower priority: hip-dominant + upper push
- Wednesday: Session B — Squat/vertical push + posterior chain accessory
- Friday: Session C — Hinge/pull focus + upper horizontal push/pull
- Optional 1–2 low-impact cardio sessions (20–30 min brisk walk, stationary bike, swimming) and daily mobility or prenatal yoga.

Phase A — Weeks 1–4: Foundation & movement quality (maintain strength, reinforce pelvic floor/midline)
Goals: reinforce good mechanics with upright and supported positions, re-establish breathing + pelvic floor coordination, maintain strength with conservative volume.

Progression rule: begin at RPE 6 for main sets. If comfortable second week, progress to RPE 6.5–7 or add 1 set or 2–4 reps. No heavy singles or doubles.

Week 1 (20 weeks pregnant — session examples)
Session A (Mon)
- Warm-up: 5–8 min bike + dynamic hips/shoulder mobility; pelvic floor breathing drill (diaphragmatic inhale, gentle pelvic floor pre-activation on exhale).
- Movement 1: Goblet squat (upright, heels elevated if needed) 3 x 8 @ RPE 6
- Movement 2: Bulgarian split squat (rear foot supported, hold DBs) 3 x 8 each leg @ RPE 6
- Push: Seated dumbbell press 3 x 8–10 @ RPE 6
- Pull: Seated cable row 3 x 8–10 @ RPE 6
- Accessory: Side-lying clams 2 x 12 each side; banded lateral walk 2 x 15 steps each way
- Core: Tall-kneeling anti-extension/Paloff press with cable/band 3 x 8–10 each side @ RPE 6
- Cool-down: gentle hamstring/quadriceps/hip flexor stretches + breathing 5 min

Session B (Wed)
- Warm-up
- Movement 1: Trap-bar deadlift (conservative load, focus on hip hinge) 3 x 6–8 @ RPE 6
- Movement 2: Step-ups (box height to maintain comfort) 3 x 8 each leg (weighted if comfortable)
- Push: Incline chest press (seated/incline bench — not supine) 3 x 8–10
- Pull: Lat pulldown (wide or neutral) 3 x 8–10
- Accessory: Single-leg Romanian deadlift (DB) 2 x 8 each
- Core: Side plank on knees 3 x 20–30s each side (or standing anti-lateral flexion with band)
- Cool-down

Session C (Fri)
- Warm-up
- Movement 1: Front rack goblet/DB squat or safety-bar squat (upright, 3 x 6–8)
- Movement 2: Cable pull-through or glute bridge variation performed upright/seated (no supine) 3 x 10
- Push: Seated machine shoulder press 3 x 8–10
- Pull: Single-arm DB row, chest-supported on incline bench 3 x 8–10 each
- Accessory: Banded pull-aparts 2 x 12; farmer carry 3 x 30–45s (weight comfortable)
- Core: Dead-bug modified (supine avoided — do tall kneeling or side-lying alternating leg lifts) 3 x 10 each side
- Cool-down

Weeks 2–4
- Maintain session structure. Progression: small load increases (2–5%) or add 1–2 reps per set as tolerated. Keep RPE 6–7. If fatigue increases, reduce volume by 1 set per lift rather than increasing intensity.

Phase B — Weeks 5–8: Strength emphasis (slightly higher intensity, continued safety)
Goals: increase mechanical load modestly to maintain/slow strength loss; introduce slightly lower rep ranges for compound moves while staying submaximal.

Progression rule: main compound lifts work at RPE 6.5–7 for 3–4 sets; keep accessory sets RPE 6. Week 5 begins around 24 weeks pregnant.

Week 5 example
Session A
- Warm-up and pelvic floor breathing
- Movement 1: Safety-bar or front squat (upright, no supine) 4 x 5–6 @ RPE 6.5
- Movement 2: Romanian deadlift (barbell or trap bar) 4 x 6–8 @ RPE 6.5
- Push: Seated DB press 3 x 8 @ RPE 6.5
- Pull: Chest-supported row 3 x 8 @ RPE 6
- Accessory: Hip abduction (cable or band) 3 x 12; glute medius work
- Core: Standing anti-rotation Pallof press 3 x 8 each side
- Cool-down

Session B
- Movement 1: Trap-bar deadlift (moderate) 4 x 4–6 @ RPE 6.5
- Movement 2: Bulgarian split squat 3 x 8–10
- Push: Seated incline press or machine chest press 3 x 6–8
- Pull: Lat pulldown 3 x 8
- Accessory: Single-leg glute bridge with bench support turned to side-lying double-leg bridge alternative if supine avoided — use seated banded glute squeeze 3 x 12
- Core: Side plank (knee or full if comfortable) 3 x 30s each side

Session C
- Movement 1: Box squat or goblet squat 4 x 6
- Movement 2: Single-arm cable row 3 x 8 each
- Push: Horizontal push (standing cable press) 3 x 8
- Pull: Face pull 3 x 12
- Accessory: Farmer carry or suitcase carry 3 x 40s
- Core: Bird-dog (quadruped) 3 x 8 each side with controlled breathing

Weeks 6–8 progression
- Increase one variable per week: either add 1 set to main lift, increase load slightly (2–5%), or add 1–2 reps. Monitor fatigue and pelvic floor symptoms. By Week 8 target main lifts at RPE ~7. Avoid sets to failure or heavy singles.

Phase C — Weeks 9–12: Maintenance and transition/prep for postpartum (increased emphasis on stability, control, and pain-free range)
Goals: maintain strength, focus on balance, mobility, and movement patterns that transfer to early postpartum rehab. Sessions become slightly lower in volume if third trimester symptoms appear.

Week 9 example (approx 28–29 weeks)
Session A
- Warm-up
- Movement 1: Safety-bar squat or goblet squat 3 x 6–8 @ RPE 6–7
- Movement 2: Romanian deadlift (lighter) 3 x 8
- Push: Seated machine press 3 x 8
- Pull: Supported single-arm row 3 x 8
- Accessory: Lateral step-downs 2 x 10 each
- Core: Standing cable anti-rotation 3 x 8 each
- Cool-down

Session B
- Movement 1: Trap-bar deadlift (lighter maintenance) 3 x 5–6
- Movement 2: Split squat or step-up 3 x 8
- Push: Incline press (seated) 3 x 8
- Pull: Lat pulldown or assisted pull-up 3 x 8
- Accessory: Glute band work 3 x 15
- Core: Modified side plank or tall-kneeling anti-extension 3 x as tolerated

Session C
- Movement 1: Single-leg Romanian deadlift 3 x 8 each
- Movement 2: Front-loaded goblet or safety-bar squat 3 x 8
- Upper superset: Seated cable row + standing single-arm cable press 3 x 8 each
- Accessory: Farmer carry or suitcase carry 3 x 30–45s
- Core/Mobility: Hip flexor release, thoracic rotation drills

Weeks 10–12 progression and taper
- Prioritize comfort. Keep loads at or below those used in Phase B unless client feels very strong — still avoid RPE 8–9. Reduce session volume in Week 12 if fatigue rises: do two sets instead of three for accessory work, keep main lifts at 2–3 sets.
- Continue pelvic floor-friendly core work. Introduce gentle diaphragmatic breathing, seated transverse abdominis activation cues, and bridging alternatives performed standing or side-lying if needed.

Sample exercise substitutions to avoid supine position
- Bench press (supine) -> Seated incline press, machine chest press, or standing cable press
- Glute bridge (supine) -> Seated banded glute squeeze, cable pull-through (upright), single-leg RDL, side-lying clam
- Dead-bug (supine) -> Quadruped bird-dog, tall-kneeling anti-extension, side-lying leg lifts
- Back extensions on Roman chair (if supine uncomfortable) -> Chest-supported incline rows or prone variations only if comfortable and not compressing abdomen; otherwise avoid.

Load and rep guidance summary
- Compound lifts: 3–4 sets of 4–8 reps at RPE 6–7 in Phases B; 3 x 6–8 in Phases A and C.
- Accessory lifts: 2–3 sets of 8–15 at RPE 5–6.
- Avoid max attempts, heavy singles, or training to failure.
- Rest 1.5–3 minutes between heavy sets; 45–90s for accessory circuits.

Nutrition and recovery recommendations
- Daily calorie needs increase during pregnancy. General guidance: aim for an extra ~200–300 kcal/day in the second trimester (tailor to pre-pregnancy BMI and activity level). Prioritize nutrient-dense food: protein ~1.2–1.8 g/kg bodyweight/day to support training and maternal/fetal needs (aim for the higher end if training hard), iron, calcium, vitamin D, omega-3 (DHA), folate and overall micronutrient adequacy. Confirm supplementation per OB recommendations.
- Protein examples: lean meats, dairy, legumes, Greek yogurt, tofu; spread protein across meals (20–40 g per meal).
- Hydration: drink regularly before, during and after sessions; avoid overheating.
- Sleep: aim for 7–9 hrs/night. Naps can be helpful if fatigue increases.
- Recovery: active recovery days, prenatal foam rolling and mobility, and pelvic floor physiotherapy consult if any concerns (pain, incontinence, pelvic heaviness). Use compression support or abdominal support garments if symptomatic.

Monitoring and when to stop training and seek care
- Stop and seek medical attention if vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, regular painful contractions, sudden swelling, severe shortness of breath, dizziness, chest pain, or decreased fetal movement occurs.
- If symptoms like urinary incontinence, pelvic heaviness, or persistent low back/pelvic pain appear, decrease load and consult pelvic-floor physiotherapist.

Notes for the trainer (practical)
- Use machines and seated variations when balance is compromised. Keep bars in front of the body rather than behind (safety-bar, trap-bar) to reduce abdominal compression.
- Cue breathing and bracing: inhale prior to eccentric, exhale through concentric while maintaining gentle pelvic floor engagement — avoid hard bearing down.
- Keep communication and symptom check-ins before, during and after sessions; be ready to scale intensity/volume daily.
- Document loads and RPE each session to progress conservatively.

Below is a practical, pregnancy-focused nutrition plan sized to support strength training and help preserve lean mass during the next 12 weeks. It’s written for general use and should be adjusted to the client’s pre-pregnancy weight, current weight gain pattern, appetite, and any medical or dietary restrictions. Encourage the client to keep regular contact with her OB or a registered dietitian if she has gestational diabetes, anemia, food intolerances, or other conditions.

Key nutrition principles (summary)
- Calories: modest increase appropriate for 2nd trimester + training. Use individualized target below.
- Protein: prioritize higher protein to support maternal lean mass and fetal needs — 1.2–1.8 g/kg bodyweight/day (lean-mass preservation target toward upper end).
- Carbohydrate: adequate to fuel training and fetal brain growth; focus on low-to-moderate GI carbs around workouts.
- Fat: include essential fats, especially omega-3 DHA (seafood or supplementation).
- Micronutrients: prioritize iron, folate, calcium, vitamin D, iodine and B12. Follow OB supplement guidance.
- Hydration: consistently hydrated; emphasize electrolytes if sessions are sweaty.
- Meal timing: spread protein across meals; include small snacks around workouts if needed.
- Weight gain: aim to follow Institute of Medicine (IOM) guidelines as a baseline, adjusted individually:
  - Normal BMI (18.5–24.9): ~11–16 kg total gain recommended
  - Underweight: higher gain; overweight: lower gain
  - Use OB guidance for target rate; we will aim for moderate steady gain consistent with maintaining lean mass and healthy fetal growth.

Step 1 — Estimate daily calorie target (example method)
- If you know her pre-pregnancy weight, use that. If not available, trainer should ask client.
- Rough method (for a general example): estimate Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE) from pre-pregnancy weight, then add ~200–300 kcal/day for 2nd trimester while training.
  - Sedentary TDEE baseline + training: multiply Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) by activity factor. For ease, use Mifflin-St Jeor or quick estimate: 20–25 kcal/kg for women with regular strength training. Then add 200–300 kcal for pregnancy.
  - Example: 70 kg pre-pregnancy client training regularly:
    - Maintenance: 25 kcal/kg × 70 kg = 1750 kcal (this is conservative RMR-based; many active people will be higher) — better to estimate TDEE = 30 kcal/kg × 70 = 2100 kcal.
    - Add pregnancy second trimester: +250 kcal → ~2350 kcal/day.
- Adjust up or down based on weight trajectory: aim for steady, guideline-consistent gain. If she’s losing weight unintentionally or losing lean mass, increase calories by 200–300 kcal and raise protein. If gaining too quickly, reduce by 100–200 kcal.

Step 2 — Protein target
- Target 1.4–1.8 g/kg/day. For a 70 kg client that’s ~98–126 g protein/day.
- Spread protein across 3–5 feedings (e.g., 25–30 g per meal + protein-rich snacks).
- High-quality sources: lean meat, poultry, fish (low-mercury choices), dairy, eggs, legumes, tofu, tempeh, protein powders if desired (whey, pea, hydrolyzed, per OB approval).

Step 3 — Carbohydrate and fat
- Carbs: 40–55% of energy can be reasonable. Focus on whole grains, fruit, starchy vegetables, and timing carbs around workouts (pre-workout small carb + protein snack; post-workout carb + protein to aid recovery).
  - Example pre-workout: banana + 8–12 g protein 30–60 min before session.
  - Example post-workout: Greek yogurt + berries, or smoothie with milk and protein powder.
- Fats: 25–35% of energy. Include 1–2 servings of oily fish/week (low mercury: salmon, sardines) or a prenatal DHA supplement providing ~200–300 mg DHA/day if fish intake is low. Include sources of unsaturated fats: avocado, olive oil, nuts/seeds.

Step 4 — Micronutrients and supplements (coordinate with OB)
- Continue prenatal vitamin with folic acid and recommended minerals.
- Iron: many pregnant people need supplemental iron. Include iron-rich foods (red meat, poultry, legumes, fortified cereals) and vitamin C with plant iron sources to enhance absorption. Have hemoglobin/iron studies checked as recommended.
- Calcium: aim for ~1000 mg/day (dairy, fortified plant milks).
- Vitamin D: 600–800 IU/day at minimum; more if deficient per bloodwork.
- Iodine: 150 mcg/day (prenatal vitamin often contains iodine).
- Omega-3 (DHA): 200–300 mg/day if not getting from fish — many OBs recommend this for fetal brain development.
- Avoid high-mercury fish (swordfish, king mackerel), raw/undercooked fish or meats, unpasteurized dairy, excessive vitamin A (retinol).

Step 5 — Meal templates and sample day (calorie/protein-matched)
Below are two sample day templates — adjust portion sizes to meet her calorie/protein target. Use the earlier calorie estimate (e.g., 2300–2500 kcal/day and 100–120 g protein for a 70 kg active client) as a guide.

Sample Day A (~2300–2500 kcal; ~110–120 g protein)
- Breakfast (approx 450–550 kcal; 25–30 g protein)
  - Greek yogurt (200–250 g) with 40–50 g oats, 1 tbsp nut butter, berries, cinnamon.
- Mid-morning snack (200–250 kcal; 15–20 g protein)
  - Smoothie: 1 scoop whey or plant protein, 150 ml milk or fortified plant milk, 1 small banana, ice.
- Lunch (approx 600 kcal; 30–35 g protein)
  - Quinoa/brown rice bowl with 120–150 g grilled chicken or tofu, mixed veg, 1/4 avocado, olive oil/lemon dressing.
- Pre-workout snack (150–200 kcal; 8–12 g protein)
  - Rice cake + 1 tbsp nut butter + small cottage cheese/cheese stick OR banana + 100 g low-fat yogurt.
- Post-workout / Afternoon snack (200–300 kcal; 15–20 g protein)
  - Tuna on whole-grain toast or hummus + whole-wheat pita + carrot sticks OR protein shake + piece of fruit.
- Dinner (approx 600–700 kcal; 25–30 g protein)
  - Baked salmon (approx 100–120 g) or lean steak/poultry, sweet potato, mixed veg, salad with olive oil.
- Evening snack if needed (100–200 kcal)
  - Cottage cheese with berries, handful of nuts, or milk + cereal.

Sample Day B (higher carb around training)
- Pre-breakfast small snack if training early: 1 slice toast + peanut butter.
- Breakfast: Omelette (2–3 eggs + spinach + mushrooms), 2 slices whole-grain toast, orange.
- Lunch: Lentil soup with lean turkey/chicken and whole-grain roll, side salad.
- Snack: Greek yogurt + granola + fruit.
- Dinner: Stir-fry with tofu or shrimp, brown rice, mixed veg.
- Evening snack: smoothie or milk + nut butter.

Step 6 — Practical strategies for lean-mass maintenance
- Prioritize protein at each eating occasion; aim for 25–35 g per meal.
- Time protein + carbs around training: small carb+protein pre-workout, full recovery meal within 1–2 hrs after training.
- Strength training stimulus: keep challenging loads regularly (as per the 12-week program) — that stimulus is critical to maintain lean mass.
- Avoid long fasts; maintain steady energy intake throughout the day to prevent muscle catabolism.
- If appetite is low: use calorie- and protein-dense liquid options (smoothies with milk, yogurt, protein powder, nut butter) and more frequent small meals.
- If experiencing nausea or food aversions: prioritize tolerable protein sources (yogurt, eggs, soups, smoothies) and simple carbs; maintain hydration.

Step 7 — Hydration, sodium and electrolytes
- Drink before, during and after sessions. Aim for at least 2.0–2.5 L fluid/day as a baseline; more with sweating or high temperatures.
- Include electrolytes (salt, potassium from fruit) if workouts are longer or cause heavy sweating.
- Avoid excessive caffeine. Most guidelines allow up to 200 mg caffeine/day; coordinate with OB.

Step 8 — Monitoring and adjustments
- Track weight gain trajectory every 1–2 weeks and energy levels, hunger, nausea, constipation, and sleep quality.
- If weight gain is too rapid for her OB-recommended target, reduce overall calories modestly (100–200 kcal/day) and reassess. If weight gain is too slow or she’s losing weight, increase calories by 200–300 kcal/day with extra protein and energy-dense snacks.
- Consider a 3-day food log and brief macronutrient analysis if more precise adjustments are needed.
- Referral: consider referring to an RD specializing in prenatal nutrition for personalized meal planning if needed.

Food safety reminders
- Avoid unpasteurized dairy and deli meats unless heated, raw or undercooked eggs and fish, and high-mercury fish.
- Wash produce thoroughly.
- Follow OB guidance on supplements and specific restrictions.

Quick checklist for you to give the client
- Target calories: example 2300–2500 kcal/day (adjust to her weight/activity).
- Protein: 1.4–1.8 g/kg/day (aim ~100–120 g/day for a 70 kg client).
- Spread protein across meals (25–35 g/meal).
- Include a DHA source (200–300 mg/day), iron-rich foods, calcium and vitamin D.
- Pre/post workout: small carb + protein before; protein + carb recovery after.
- Hydrate, avoid supine, avoid high-mercury/unsafe foods, follow OB supplementation.

If you want, I can:
- Convert this to a day-by-day 7-day meal plan with grocery list tailored to her calorie and protein targets (send me her pre-pregnancy weight or current weight and dietary preferences/allergies).
- Calculate exact calorie and macronutrient targets using her weight and activity factor and produce portion sizes and recipes.

Below is a progressive, pregnancy-safe cardio plan to add to the 12-week strength program you already have for your 30‑year‑old, advanced lifter at 20 weeks gestation. It follows the same conservative principles: no high-impact or contact sports, avoid overheating, watch balance changes, stop for any warning signs (see below), and prioritize perceived exertion over heart‑rate targets. The plan is adaptable to her daily symptoms and energy levels and complements the strength work and nutrition plan to help preserve conditioning and cardiovascular health.

Key safety reminders (read first)
- Stop exercise and contact OB if she experiences vaginal bleeding, regular painful contractions, chest pain, dizziness, fainting, sudden severe shortness of breath, decreased fetal movement, or fluid leakage.
- Avoid overheating — especially in hot/humid environments. Prefer cool gym, early morning or evening, and ensure hydration.
- Avoid high-impact/jarring activities and abrupt direction changes. No contact sports or activities with fall risk.
- Avoid supine positions after week 16; use upright/seated versions of cardio equipment.
- Monitor RPE: aim mostly for RPE 5–7/10 for moderate sessions, occasional 7–8/10 for short intervals only if tolerated and cleared by OB.
- Keep sessions manageable: 2–4 cardio sessions per week depending on energy: 20–40 minutes each, varying intensity and modality.

Overview and weekly structure
- Frequency: 2–3 planned cardio sessions per week (plus optional light activity on other days). Combine with strength days: do cardio after strength or on separate days depending on fatigue.
- Session duration: 20–40 minutes depending on intensity and tolerance.
- Intensity model: use RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion) and talk-test. Most work at moderate intensity (can talk but not sing). Occasional short higher-effort intervals allowed (RPE 7–8) but keep conservative and brief.
- Modalities: treadmill walking (incline), stationary bike (recumbent or upright), elliptical (low impact), swimming/aquatic exercise, rowing (if comfortable with torso position), stairmill (careful with balance), walking outdoors, or cardio machines in a seated/standing supported position.
- Progression: progress volume first (add 5–10 min), then add incline/resistance or short interval efforts only if comfortable. Avoid pushing to high intensity or maximal work.

Cardio periodization by phase (aligned with 12-week strength phases)
- Phase A (Weeks 1–4): Establish baseline, moderate steady-state cardio 2×/week (20–30 min), plus 1 optional gentle session (walking/swim)
- Phase B (Weeks 5–8): Slight increase in volume and optional short intervals 2×/week moderate steady + 1× optional interval session (total 2–3 sessions)
- Phase C (Weeks 9–12): Maintain cardio, prioritize comfort and recovery, reduce volume if fatigue—2×/week steady or light intervals; include aquatic sessions as tolerance declines.

Week-by-week cardio plan (session templates)
Weeks 1–4 (Phase A) — baseline conditioning
Goal: maintain aerobic fitness and support recovery and mood. RPE 5–6 most sessions.

Week 1–2 (example)
- Session 1 (Mon or same day as strength if after lifting): Treadmill brisk walk with incline
  - 5–8 min warm-up easy walking (RPE 3–4)
  - 20 min brisk walk at RPE 5–6; use 3–6% incline or slight speed increase to raise effort without impact
  - 5 min cool-down easy walking + gentle stretching
- Session 2 (Thu): Pool-based or stationary bike
  - 5–8 min warm-up
  - 20–30 min continuous stationary bike (recumbent if comfort needed) at RPE 4.5–6
  - Optional: include 3 × 30–45s faster efforts at RPE 7 with 2–3 min easy between (only if tolerated)
  - Cool-down 5 min
- Optional Session 3 (Sun): 20–30 min easy walk or prenatal yoga/longer pool session for recovery (RPE 3–4)

Week 3–4
- Slightly increase one session by +5–10 minutes (e.g., one 30-min walk). Keep intensity mostly moderate.

Weeks 5–8 (Phase B) — maintain with optional intervals
Goal: gently increase cardiovascular stimulus while monitoring fatigue. RPE mostly 5–7; include short interval work if client feels good and cleared.

Week 5–6 (example)

Even though she’s an advanced lifter and cleared for moderate strength work, pregnancy guidance is to avoid maximal efforts, Valsalva, and heavy, near‑maximal single reps because of increased cardiovascular strain, intra‑abdominal pressure, pelvic floor load, and balance/fall risk.

Why not test a 1RM while pregnant
- Cardiovascular stress: maximal efforts spike heart rate and blood pressure more than submaximal work. Pregnancy already increases cardiac output and blood volume; avoiding extreme acute spikes is prudent.
- Intra‑abdominal and pelvic‑floor load: maximal lifts typically involve heavy bracing and Valsalva which significantly increase intra‑abdominal pressure and place stress on the pelvic floor and the linea alba (diastasis recti risk).
- Balance and fall risk: a failed maximal attempt or a very heavy lift increases the risk of loss of balance or injury; center of gravity changes as pregnancy progresses.
- Fetal considerations: while evidence is limited and routine submaximal resistance is generally safe with OB clearance, maximal lifting adds unnecessary and avoidable risk without clinical benefit.
- Clinical guidance: most obstetric and exercise medicine sources recommend avoiding maximal exertion testing and maximal lifts; instead use submaximal testing and validated estimations.

Safe alternatives to a 1RM to satisfy her desire to “feel like she’s testing”
1) Submaximal rep‑to‑failure test with RPE cap (estimate 1RM)
- Use a heavy but submaximal set at RPE ≤ 8 for a multi‑rep test (e.g., 3–6 reps). Example: perform a 3‑rep max (3RM) at RPE 7–8 (not a true maximal, stop if it would reach 9–10), then estimate 1RM with conservative formulas. This keeps intensity high without an all‑out single.
- Better: limit to 3–5 rep top sets at RPE 7–8 and use those numbers for estimated 1RM. Stop if breathing becomes strained or pelvic pressure increases.

2) Velocity or bar speed testing (if gym has tools)
- Use bar speed to track relative intensity: perform a set at a known submaximal weight and measure concentric velocity. Changes in speed can indicate strength changes without maximal loading. This is low risk and informative for advanced lifters.

3) Rep‑range progression with a scheduled “heavy but safe” top set
- On her peak week, program heavier top working sets at RPE 7–8 for 3–5 reps on primary lifts (e.g., seated incline press, trap‑bar deadlift) rather than singles. Ensure longer rest (2.5–3.5 min) and strict breathing cues. This gives a strong training stimulus and the subjective feeling of a peak without the risk of a 1RM.

4) Use isometric or eccentric overload tests (lower risk)
- Isometric mid‑range holds or controlled slow eccentrics at submaximal loads can feel very challenging and provide measurable progress while reducing ballistic risk.

5) Strength markers other than 1RM
- Track increases in volume‑load (sets × reps × weight), decreases in RPE at a given weight, or ability to complete a heavier submaximal top set for prescribed reps. These are valid performance indicators and safer.

If you still want a testing plan for week 12, here’s a safe “peak” protocol you can use instead of a 1RM:
- Goal: produce a high‑intensity training stimulus and estimate 1RM without a true maximal attempt.
- Preconditions: client must feel well that day, no pelvic pressure, OB still cleared, and she must agree to stop immediately if breathlessness, dizziness, or pelvic symptoms occur.

Week 12 safe peak protocol (example)
- Warm-up thoroughly: 8–12 minutes general + specific progressive sets for the lift, practice breathing/pelvic‑floor coordination.
- Choose 2 primary lifts to “peak” (e.g., trap‑bar deadlift and seated incline press) — avoid any flat supine bench.
- Work-up plan for each lift (no singles to failure)
  - Set 1: 6 reps @ RPE 6 (light)
  - Set 2: 4 reps @ RPE 6.5 (moderate)
  - Set 3: 3 reps @ RPE 7 (challenging but controlled)
  - Set 4 (top working): 3 reps @ RPE 7.5–8 — stop here; do NOT attempt heavier single reps. Use this top set as your “test” and estimate a 1RM from the 3RM using conservative equations if desired.
  - If RPE would exceed 8, stop the progression.
- Rest 2.5–3.5 min between these heavier sets; monitor breathing and pelvic signs.
- Do no more than two maximal (submaximal) top sets across the entire session.
- For accessory pressing, keep sets moderate (3 × 6–8 @ RPE 6–7).
- After session: cool-down, gentle pelvic‑floor breathing and hydration.

How to estimate 1RM from a submaximal top set (conservative)
- Use a 3‑rep value at RPE ≤ 8 and apply a conservative multiplier (e.g., estimated 1RM ≈ weight × 1.06–1.10 for a 3RM at <9 RPE). Do not chase the number; use it purely for tracking.

Final recommendation
- Do not test a real 1RM while pregnant.
- Use one of the safer alternatives above so she still feels challenged and can track progress.
- If she absolutely insists, explain the risks clearly and advise deferring true 1RM testing until postpartum (once cleared by OB and pelvic‑floor specialist). Postpartum testing can be scheduled once she has adequate pelvic‑floor recovery and medical clearance.

Quick client details / constraints
- 30 y/o, advanced lifter, 20 weeks pregnant (OB cleared for moderate strength).
- Contraindications: no supine after week 16, no max attempts (no true 1RM), no contact sports.
- Goals: maintain/slow strength loss, preserve lean mass, keep pressing (bench-feel) and strong core, maintain conditioning.

Program overview (structure)
- Duration: 12 weeks (Phase A Weeks 1–4; Phase B Weeks 5–8; Phase C Weeks 9–12).
- Frequency: 3 gym strength sessions/week (Mon/Wed/Fri suggested) + 2–3 cardio sessions/week (can be done on non-lift days or after lifting at reduced duration).
- Session length: ~45–60 minutes for strength; cardio 20–40 minutes per session.
- Intensity model: RPE-based. Avoid RPE 9–10 and no true 1RM or maximal singles. Heavy top sets in Phase B allowed up to RPE 7–7.5 (occasionally 8 if all safety checks pass).
- Core: short 8–15 minute core circuit after each strength session (standing/tall‑kneeling/quadruped/side‑lying variations only).
- Nutrition: calorie increase for 2nd trimester (+~200–300 kcal/day baseline, tailor to weight/activity), protein 1.4–1.8 g/kg/day, spread protein across meals, ensure prenatal vitamins, DHA, iron/calcium/Vit D as advised by OB. Hydrate and prioritize recovery.
- Cardio: 2–3 low‑impact sessions/week (treadmill incline walking, recumbent bike, elliptical, pool/aquatics). RPE 5–6 mostly; short intervals (RPE 7–7.5) only in Phase B if tolerated.

Progression rules (general)
- Progress conservatively: increase reps, sets, or load by small increments (2–5%) when current work is RPE ≤ 6 for two sessions.
- Prefer increasing volume before intensity. Keep rest 1.5–3 min for compound lifts; 45–90s for accessories.
- Monitor pelvic pressure, urinary leakage, dizziness, bleeding — stop and consult OB if any adverse sign occurs.

Phase A — Foundation & movement quality (Weeks 1–4) — 20–24 weeks gestation
Goal: retain movement quality, breathing/pelvic‑floor coordination, baseline strength.

Weekly pattern (Mon/Wed/Fri)
- Warm-up: 8–10 min bike/walk + shoulder/thoracic mobility + pelvic‑floor breathing
- Main lifts: 2–3 compound moves per session. RPE target main lifts 6–6.5
  - Examples: Goblet squat 3x8; Bulgarian split squat 3x8; Trap‑bar deadlift 3x6–8
- Upper push/pull: Seated DB press 3x8–10; Seated cable row 3x8–10; Incline chest press seated 3x8–10
- Accessories: banded lateral walks, clams, single‑leg RDL 2–3x8–12
- Core (post‑session): tall‑kneeling Pallof 3x8–10 each side; quadruped bird‑dog 3x8 each; side plank on knees 3x15–20s each
- Cardio: 2 sessions/week 20–30 min moderate walking or pool

Phase B — Strength & push emphasis (Weeks 5–8) — 24–28 weeks gestation
Goal: increase pushing intensity and bench‑pattern work, maintain other strength. Keep top RPE submaximal (7–7.5). Include bench-substitutes (seated/incline/landmine).

Weekly pattern (Mon/Wed/Fri) — heavy push on Mon (Session A)
- Warm-up: 8–10 min + mobility + pelvic‑floor breathing
- Session A — Heavy Push Emphasis (Mon)
  - Seated incline DB/barbell press (back supported) 4–5 × 4–6 @ RPE 7–7.5
  - Single‑arm landmine/cable chest press 3 × 6–8 each side @ RPE 7
  - Seated machine chest press 3 × 6–8 @ RPE 7
  - Antagonist: Seated cable row 3 × 8–10
  - Accessories: triceps ext. 3 × 8–12; lateral raises 2 × 10–12
  - Core: standing/tall‑kneeling Pallof press 3–4 × 8–10 each side; farmer carry 3 × 30–60s
- Session B — Lower/hyp/hinge (Wed)
  - Trap‑bar deadlift 4 × 4–6 @ RPE 6.5
  - Bulgarian split squat 3 × 8–10
  - Lat pulldown 3 × 8–10
  - Light seated chest press 2 × 8
  - Core: standing single‑arm cable anti‑rotation 3 × 8 each; side plank on knees 3 × 20–30s
- Session C — Full body/press maintenance (Fri)
  - Front-loaded goblet or safety‑bar squat 3 × 6–8
  - Chest‑supported single‑arm row 3 × 8 each
  - Standing cable incline press / chest‑supported incline press 3 × 5–6 @ RPE 7
  - Face pulls, farmer carries, posterior chain accessory work
  - Core: banded anti‑extension 3 × 8–10; loaded bird‑dog 3 × 8 each
- Cardio: 2–3 sessions/week (one interval session permitted with short efforts 30–60s at RPE 7) — total moderate work 25–35 min

Phase B progression notes
- Increase load modestly (2–5%) or add a set or 1–2 reps weekly if RPE remains ≤ 6–7.
- Heavy push top sets targeted RPE 7–7.5 (rarely 8). Avoid RPE 9–10 and any heavy single attempts.
- Maintain pelvic‑floor checks, lengthen rest between heavy push sets (2–3 min).

Phase C — Maintenance & preparation for postpartum (Weeks 9–12) — 28–32 weeks gestation
Goal: maintain strength and control; prioritize comfort, mobility, and core endurance. Peak week uses safe submaximal test instead of 1RM.

Weekly pattern (Mon/Wed/Fri)
- Warm-up and breathing as before
- Lifts: keep main lifts at 3 sets × 6–8 @ RPE 6–7; reduce overall volume if fatigue rises
  - Example: Safety‑bar/goblet squat 3 × 6–8; Trap‑bar deadlift 3 × 5–6; Single‑leg RDL 3 × 8; Seated incline press 3 × 6–8
- Press maintenance across sessions with seated/incline presses, landmine presses and cable work
- Accessories: posterior chain, glute medius and shoulder health work; farmer carries for core endurance
- Core: maintain Pallof presses, side planks, bird‑dogs, anti‑extension work (2–3 exercises per session)
- Cardio: prefer pool/aqua (excellent late pregnancy), recumbent bike or walking 20–30 min; reduce intervals — mostly moderate

Week 12 — Peak week (safe protocol; no 1RM)
- Do NOT perform a true 1RM. Use a conservative peak protocol:
  - Warm-up thoroughly.
  - Choose up to 2 primary lifts (e.g., trap‑bar deadlift and seated incline press).
  - Work-up: 6 × 6 @ RPE 6, 4 × 4 @ RPE 6.5, 3 × 3 @ RPE 7, top set 3 reps @ RPE 7.5–8 (stop there). No singles, no maximal attempts.
  - Use top 3‑rep as estimate for progress tracking; estimate 1RM conservatively (e.g., 3RM × 1.06).
  - Keep rest 2.5–3.5 min between heavier sets; monitor symptoms.
- Reduce accessory volume; emphasize recovery, mobility and pelvic‑floor breathing post-session.

Core program (integrated each strength day; 8–15 min)
- Phase A: tall‑kneeling Pallof press, quadruped bird‑dog, side plank on knees (3× per exercise)
- Phase B: heavier Pallof presses (cable), banded anti‑extension rollouts (tall kneel), farmer/suitcase carries, loaded bird‑dog (3–4×)
- Phase C: maintenance core — standing Pallof, side plank variations, bird‑dog, carries (moderate volume)
- Daily pelvic‑floor breathing drills (2–3 min) and small quick gentle pelvic‑floor activations (6–8 quick flicks) — avoid forced max holds.

Cardio plan (2–3 sessions/week)
- Phase A: 2 sessions × 20–30 min moderate (incline treadmill walk, recumbent bike, pool)
- Phase B: 2–3 sessions × 25–35 min with optional short intervals (30–60s at RPE 7) only if tolerated
- Phase C: 2 sessions × 20–30 min prioritizing pool/aqua and walking; reduce intensity if fatigue rises
- Use talk test and RPE (moderate = 5–6/10). Hydrate and avoid overheating.

Nutrition & recovery (summary)
- Calories: increase ~200–300 kcal/day in 2nd trimester as baseline; adjust to weight gain guidance and activity. Monitor weight gain every 1–2 weeks and adjust ±100–300 kcal as needed.
- Protein: 1.4–1.8 g/kg/day (aim for upper end to preserve lean mass). Spread across meals (25–35 g protein/meal).
- Carbs/fats: fuel workouts with 30–60 g carbs around sessions; include healthy fats and DHA (200–300 mg/day from fish/supplement).
- Micronutrients: prenatal vitamin, iron as needed, calcium ~1000 mg/day, vitamin D per OB, iodine as recommended.
- Hydration: ≥2–2.5 L baseline; more with sweat. Avoid overheating, keep cool environment.
- Sleep: 7–9 hours; naps if needed. Recovery between heavy push days: 48–72 hours ideal.
- Refer to pelvic‑floor physio for any incontinence, pelvic pain, diastasis concerns.

Safety & red flags (stop exercise and seek care)
- Vaginal bleeding, regular painful contractions, decreased fetal movement, chest pain, sudden severe shortness of breath, dizziness/fainting, sudden severe swelling, or fluid leakage.
- New or worsening pelvic heaviness, urinary incontinence, or sharp pelvic/abdominal pain — reduce load and consult pelvic health professional.

- Never supine after week 16: use supported incline/seated options for presses and chest work.
- No heavy Valsalva: inhale on eccentric, exhale on concentric while maintaining gentle pelvic‑floor engagement.
- Progress conservatively; small increases in load or reps weekly if RPE allows.
- Document RPE, loads and symptoms each session.
- Use machines and chest‑supported variations for heavier work when balance is a concern.
- Use a spotter for heavier seated/incline barbell work if available and safe.

Testing & postpartum plan
- No true 1RM testing during pregnancy. Use submaximal 3–5 rep top sets to estimate 1RM if desired.
- Plan formal 1RM testing postpartum only after OB clearance and pelvic‑floor rehab as needed (commonly 3–6+ months postpartum depending on recovery).
